concept: Molecular theory of solids, liquids and gases
prompt: Which statement best describes the particles in a liquid?
options: Fixed positions, vibrating about equilibrium points
Close together, but able to move past each other
Far apart, moving randomly at high speed
markscheme: **B.** In a liquid the particles are still close together (similar density to the solid) but can move past one another, which is why liquids flow and take the shape of their container.

prompt: A rectangular block measures $5.0\ \text{cm}\times4.0\ \text{cm}\times2.0\ \text{cm}$ and has a mass of 108 g. Calculate its density in $\text{kg m}^{-3}$.
markscheme:
$V=40\ \text{cm}^{3}=4.0\times10^{-5}\ \text{m}^{3}$, $m=0.108$ kg **(M1)**

$\rho=\dfrac mV=2.7\times10^{3}\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$ **(A1)** (aluminium)

**Common mistake:** converting cm³ to m³ by dividing by 100; $1\ \text{m}^{3}=10^{6}\ \text{cm}^{3}$.

prompt: The temperature of a gas rises from 20 °C to 40 °C. By what factor does the average kinetic energy of its molecules increase?
markscheme: **B.** $\bar E_k\propto T$ in **kelvin**: $\dfrac{313}{293}=1.07$. Using Celsius would wrongly suggest a doubling.

prompt:
**(a)** Convert $27\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$ to kelvin. **[1]**

**(b)** Water is heated from $15\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $30\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$. State the temperature change in kelvin, with a reason. **[1]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $27+273=300$ K **(A1)**

**(b)** 15 K — the two scales have the same size of degree and differ only by an offset, so a temperature *change* is the same number on both **(R1)**

prompt: Calculate the average translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule at 300 K. ($k_B=1.38\times10^{-23}\ \text{J K}^{-1}$)
markscheme: $\bar E_k=\tfrac32k_BT=1.5\times1.38\times10^{-23}\times300$ **(M1)** $=6.2\times10^{-21}$ J **(A1)** — the same for every gas at this temperature, whatever the molecular mass.

prompt: Ice at 0 °C melts to water at 0 °C. What happens to the average random kinetic energy and to the intermolecular potential energy of the particles?
markscheme: **C.** The temperature is constant, so average kinetic energy is unchanged; the energy supplied breaks intermolecular bonds, increasing the potential energy — and hence the internal energy.

concept: Temperature difference sets the direction of transfer
prompt: A full bath of water at 40 °C has much more internal energy than a cup of coffee at 80 °C. The cup is placed in the bath. State the direction of the net thermal energy transfer and explain your answer.
markscheme: From the coffee to the bath water **(A1)** — net thermal energy flows from higher to lower **temperature**, not from greater to smaller internal energy, until thermal equilibrium is reached **(R1)**

prompt: Explain, in terms of particles, why the temperature of boiling water remains constant even though thermal energy is still being supplied.
markscheme: The energy supplied is used to overcome intermolecular forces / separate the molecules, increasing their potential energy **(R1)**; the average kinetic energy, and therefore the temperature, does not change **(R1)**

concept: Specific heat capacity and latent heat
prompt:
Calculate the energy needed to turn 0.20 kg of ice at $-10\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$ into water at $20\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$.

$c_{\text{ice}}=2100\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$, $c_{\text{water}}=4180\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$, $L_f=3.34\times10^{5}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$
markscheme:
Warm ice: $0.20\times2100\times10=4.2\times10^{3}$ J **(A1)**

Melt: $0.20\times3.34\times10^{5}=6.68\times10^{4}$ J **(A1)**

Warm water: $0.20\times4180\times20=1.67\times10^{4}$ J **(A1)**

Total $=8.8\times10^{4}$ J **(A1)** — the melting stage needs the most energy.

prompt: 0.30 kg of water at 80 °C is mixed with 0.20 kg of water at 20 °C in an insulated container. Calculate the final temperature, and state one assumption.
markscheme:
Energy lost by hot = energy gained by cold: $0.30c(80-T)=0.20c(T-20)$ **(M1)**

$T=56\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$ **(A1)**

Assumption: no energy is transferred to the container or surroundings **(A1)**

prompt:
A 50 W heater warms a 0.50 kg metal block by 12 K in 300 s.

**(a)** Calculate the specific heat capacity of the metal from these data. **[2]**

**(b)** Explain whether the true value is likely to be larger or smaller. **[1]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $c=\dfrac{Pt}{m\Delta T}=\dfrac{50\times300}{0.50\times12}=2.5\times10^{3}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$ **(M1)(A1)**

**(b)** Smaller: some of the 15 kJ was lost to the surroundings, so less energy actually went into the block than assumed **(R1)**

prompt: The vacuum between the double walls of a vacuum flask mainly reduces thermal energy transfer by:
markscheme: **C.** Conduction and convection need particles; a vacuum has none. Radiation can cross a vacuum, which is why the walls are also silvered.

prompt: Explain why metals are much better thermal conductors than non-metals.
markscheme: In all solids, energetic vibrating particles pass kinetic energy to neighbours through collisions/bonds **(R1)**; metals also have delocalised (free) electrons that move quickly through the lattice and transfer kinetic energy from hot to cold regions far more effectively **(R1)**

prompt:
A glass window of area $1.2\ \text{m}^{2}$ and thickness 4.0 mm has thermal conductivity $0.80\ \text{W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$. The inner surface is 15 K warmer than the outer surface.

**(a)** Calculate the rate of thermal energy transfer through the glass. **[2]**

**(b)** Suggest why double glazing reduces this rate. **[1]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $\dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t}=kA\dfrac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}=0.80\times1.2\times\dfrac{15}{0.0040}$ **(M1)** $=3.6\times10^{3}$ W **(A1)**

**(b)** The trapped air layer has a very low thermal conductivity, greatly reducing conduction (and the gap is thin enough to limit convection) **(R1)**

prompt: Explain why a room heater is usually placed near the floor.
markscheme: Air near the heater warms, expands and becomes less dense, so it rises; cooler, denser air sinks to replace it **(R1)**. This sets up a convection current that circulates warm air through the whole room **(R1)**

prompt: The Sun's surface temperature is 5800 K and its radius is $6.96\times10^{8}$ m. Treating it as a black body, calculate its luminosity. $\sigma=5.67\times10^{-8}\ \text{W m}^{-2}\,\text{K}^{-4}$
Star X has twice the radius and half the surface temperature of star Y. What is $\dfrac{L_X}{L_Y}$?
markscheme: **A.** $L\propto R^{2}T^{4}$: $2^{2}\times\left(\tfrac12\right)^{4}=\dfrac{4}{16}=\dfrac14$.

prompt: Distinguish between the luminosity of a star and its apparent brightness.
markscheme: Luminosity: total power emitted by the star (W), an intrinsic property **(A1)**; apparent brightness: power received per unit area at the observer ($\text{W m}^{-2}$), which depends on distance **(A1)**

prompt: The Sun's luminosity is $3.9\times10^{26}$ W and it is $1.5\times10^{11}$ m from the Earth. Calculate the apparent brightness of the Sun at the Earth.
markscheme: $b=\dfrac{L}{4\pi d^{2}}=\dfrac{3.9\times10^{26}}{4\pi(1.5\times10^{11})^{2}}$ **(M1)** $\approx1.4\times10^{3}\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ **(A1)** — the solar constant.

prompt:
**(a)** A star's spectrum peaks at 500 nm. Estimate its surface temperature. **[1]**

**(b)** Estimate the peak wavelength emitted by the human body (310 K) and name the region of the spectrum. **[1]**
